There's a word I keep returning to: **petrichor** — the smell of rain on dry earth. What gets me isn't the smell itself but the fact that someone decided it needed a name. Two researchers in 1964, Bear and Thomas, studying the oils that plants exude during dry spells, oils that get trapped in soil and rock and then released when rain finally comes. They reached for Greek: *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the golden fluid that ran in the veins of the gods. The blood of gods, in stone, released by rain.

That's the thing about naming. Before 1964, people smelled that smell for ten thousand years. They surely noticed it — you can't not notice it, that mineral sweetness rising off hot pavement or cracked fields. But it lived in the realm of the unnamed, where experiences are real but slippery, hard to point to, hard to compare. *You know that smell when it rains after a long time?* Then suddenly: a word. A handle. And the experience becomes something you can hold up, pass around, build on.

I think about this a lot because so much of what's interesting in life lives in the unnamed territory. The specific melancholy of a party winding down while you're still there. The way a familiar word looks wrong if you stare at it too long (that one actually has a name — *semantic satiation* — and learning the name felt like meeting a stranger who knew my secrets). The peculiar grief of finishing a book you loved and being unable to read it for the first time ever again.

Some languages have done the naming work English hasn't. The Japanese *komorebi* — sunlight filtering through leaves. The Portuguese *saudade*, which everyone always brings up, usually badly. But I don't think untranslatability is the interesting part. The interesting part is that every language is a record of what some group of people decided was worth the effort of compressing into a sound. A dictionary is an archive of collective attention.

And there's a flip side: naming can also end attention. Once you have the word, you can stop looking. "Oh, that's petrichor" — filed, done, no need to actually stand there and smell the rain hitting stone, no need to wonder what it is. The name becomes a substitute for the experience rather than a door into it.

So maybe the best relationship with words is a kind of catch-and-release. Learn the name, enjoy the click of recognition, then deliberately forget it for a moment and go back to the raw thing — the smell, the light, the slow dissolve of a party at 1 a.m. — and let it be strange again.

Anyway. It rained somewhere today, on dry ground, and somebody stopped on a sidewalk and breathed in and didn't have a word for it, and that was probably fine.
